Guanajuato is known for its multicolored houses climbing the hills around the historic center. Its narrow streets and underground roads make the city's unusual layout especially apparent as you explore on foot. Squares, churches and buildings connected with Mexico's cultural life have been preserved here.

Notable sights include the Juárez Theatre, the basilica and Plaza de la Paz. The Alley of the Kiss is associated with a local romantic legend. Guanajuato is rewarding both for its panoramic views and for smaller details: the colors of its facades, stairways between neighborhoods and squares where daily city life continues.

Guatapé is known for houses with brightly colored facades and relief designs along the lower parts of their walls. These decorative panels depict scenes of everyday life and turn a simple walk through the streets into an attraction in its own right. The details are best viewed up close: each house has its own combination of colors and subjects.

Nearby rises the rock of El Peñón de Guatapé. From the top, a different view of the surrounding area opens up, with water, low hills and numerous islands. Visiting the rock adds another dimension to exploring the town; after the climb, you can return to a leisurely walk and stop for coffee at a local café.

Guatavita is a pleasant place to pause after visiting the lake of the same name. White facades, tiled roofs and small squares give the town a distinctive, unified appearance. You can stroll through the streets and browse local shops before continuing your journey around Bogotá.

The town is in the department of Cundinamarca. It is often included in day trips from the capital along with Lake Guatavita and the Salt Cathedral of Zipaquirá. The town and the lake serve different purposes on an itinerary: in town, visitors explore the streets; at the lake, they discover the high-altitude natural environment and the legend of El Dorado.

The Guayabero River flows through the La Macarena area, along the route to Caño Cristales. Boat journeys on the river form part of nature excursions. From the water, you can see the riverbanks and surrounding vegetation, so the crossing itself becomes an introduction to the region's landscape.

The onward journey to the colorful river continues overland and along walking trails. The Guayabero reveals the waterborne side of this trip, complementing the rocky stretches and cascades of Caño Cristales. The river is a natural attraction in its own right in the La Macarena area, where boat trips and forest routes are closely connected.

## Malecón 2000 and Las Peñas: What to See in Guayaquil, Ecuador

### Guayaquil: Ecuador's Tourist Hub

Guayaquil is Ecuador's largest city and economic center. It owes its name to its proximity to the Guayas River. The city's full name, Santiago de Guayaquil, reflects its origins: it was founded by the Spanish conquistador Sebastián de Belalcázar.

The city seems to hover above the Pacific coastline. Guayaquil has managed to preserve a small pocket of colonial architecture within its maze of streets.

Here you can admire the buildings of the city's colonial quarter, a covered market of glass and steel, magnificent themed and botanical gardens, and numerous fountains. Guayaquil's Historic Park combines a zoo with an ethnographic museum. The coast not far from the city, with its beautiful beaches and surfing spots, also draws many visitors.

## Holidays in Guayaquil

### Guayaquil: A Beach Destination and Much More

Guayaquil offers plenty of resorts for beach lovers. Machalilla National Park is of interest for its large colonies of albatrosses and frigatebirds. In the old port of Puerto López, whales can be seen from June to September; an excellent viewing platform has been set up for this purpose.
